en: The Mahāsannipāta-ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra (Dutt 1) START Rkp 1
The First Chapter.
Homage to the Tathāgata Gandhaprabhaśrī. Homage to Mahābrahmaghoṣa.
One who pays homage to these has not encountered the array of Māra;
this dhāraṇī should be taken up.
By me, success was attained in this vidyā.
avāme avāme avāme / om vare om vare / parikuñja naṭa naṭa puṣkara vahaja lukha /
Khama khama / ili mili / kili mili.
O Kīrtivara! Seal, seal, in the mouth, svāhā!
Thus have I heard.

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the great city, at the Vyākalantaka alms-resort, together with a great saṅgha of bhikṣus— namely, one thousand bhikṣus who were all arhats, whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery,
whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were noble steeds, great elephants, who had accomplished their task and completed what was to be done.

Together with millions of bodhisattvas who had laid down their burdens, attained their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, whose minds were perfectly liberated through right knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states— seated in solitude along with that great assembly of bodhisattvas, such as the youth Meruśikharadhara and the youth Varūṇamati.

With Sumati Kumārabhūta, Jinamati Kumārabhūta, Raśmimati Kumārabhūta, Ākāśamati Kumārabhūta, Vidyunmati Kumārabhūta, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Śākyakumārabhūta, Varuṇakumārabhūta, Vimalakumārabhūta, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.

All those millions of bodhisattvas had attained the dhāraṇīs and samādhis of patience; they possessed unobstructed knowledge of all phenomena, maintained a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, and had completely transcended the domain of all Māras.
They were skilled in the knowledge of entering the domain of all Tathāgatas, endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion, and proficient in the knowledge of skillful means.
At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there lived two wise wanderers who were intelligent, masters of the eighteen branches of knowledge, and accompanied by retinues of five hundred followers.
One was Upatiṣya and the other was Kolita.
These two leaders of the groups of wanderers made an agreement with one another.
"Whichever of us two first attains the nectar of immortality must inform the other.
Then, in the forenoon, the Venerable Aśvajit dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
The wandering mendicant Upatiṣya saw the venerable Aśvajit setting out for his alms-round in the great city of Rājagṛha as he was walking for alms.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
"Never before have I seen such a pleasing deportment in any ascetic, brahmin, or any other human being as that of this monk; what if I were to approach him..."
"I would like to ask you something: Venerable sir, who is your teacher? For whose sake have you gone forth? Or whose Dharma do you find pleasing?
Then Upatiṣya approached the venerable Aśvajit; having approached and drawn near, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the venerable Aśvajit.
[He sat down at a distance.
Seated to one side, the wandering mendicant Upatiṣya said this to the venerable Aśvajit:
"Venerable sir, who is your teacher? With whom have you gone forth? Or whose Dharma do you find pleasing?"
Then the Venerable Aśvajit said this to the wanderer Upatiṣya:

"The Śākya has a son who is great in vows and asceticism, the most excellent in this world, a self-mastered one who, though having crossed to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, is himself liberated and likewise a liberator of the world."
The one called Buddha is fully awakened, supreme here, and the drier of the ocean of suffering;
having always gone to him for refuge, I am stainless, and therefore the Dharma is pleasing to me.
Upatiṣya said:
"What does your teacher profess? What does he teach? The Venerable Aśvajit replied:
Therefore, venerable one, listen well and attend thoroughly; I shall speak.

Just as the Guide has explained how the progression of the world possesses karma and afflictions along with their causes and conditions, he has likewise proclaimed the cause for the cessation of karma and afflictions.
Having personally realized that supreme liberation in which the suffering inevitably associated with birth, old age, and misfortune does not abide, that bull among speakers proclaims it.
Then, having heard this Dharma discourse, the wandering mendicant Upatiṣya attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena—stainless, free from impurity, and devoid of secondary afflictions.
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry, at that moment he spoke these verses: ... ... ... the perpetual drying up of the rivers of birth.
That nectar of the Dharma, so difficult to hear even from a Buddha, has been taught by me;
it is for the pacification of the suffering of the world, and through the incomparable manifestation of wisdom,
this path has indeed been perfected.
Then the wandering mendicant Upatiṣya said this to the venerable Aśvajit: "Where, venerable sir, does the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, reside? The venerable Aśvajit replied:

"Right here, venerable sir, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakanivāpa, together with a great community of monks—namely, the thousand matted-hair ascetics who had gone forth.
Upatiṣya said:
"Friend, having looked upon my companions along with their groups of disciples, I shall go forth."
Then the wandering mendicant Upatiṣya, having bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Aśvajit and circumambulated him three times, departed.
He went to where Kolita was;
there, the wandering mendicant Kolita saw the wandering mendicant Upatiṣya approaching from afar.
And having seen him, he said to the wandering ascetic Upatiṣya:
"Venerable sir, your faculties are serene; the color of your face is pure; the complexion of your skin is bright.
He replied:
“O Venerable One, you have attained the Deathless.
Upatiṣya said,
“Venerable One, I have attained the Deathless.”
"Venerable one, listen and attend well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you that which has been realized by me.
Then Kolita the wanderer, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground, bowed with palms joined toward Upatiṣya the wanderer and said this:
"May I cross beyond the three realms of existence, and may I destroy the flood of water and the great enemies that are the aggregates."
O Śiva, tell me that one path free from sorrow, by which I may know here [the way] to the state of no further rebirth.
Then Upatiṣya said:
"Just as the progression of the world possesses karma and afflictions as its causes and conditions,"
The Leader also proclaimed the cause for the cessation of karma and afflictions;
having himself realized that supreme liberation in which the suffering inevitably consisting of birth, old age, and death does not abide, that bull among speakers spoke of it.
Kolita also said:
"For the sake of the pacification of suffering, it is peaceful...
[it is the pacification of all defilements, turbidities, and faults of views, and it cuts through ignorance]."
Conditioned phenomena are hollow, empty, void, and deceptive; speak further, therefore, of that stainless word which, upon hearing, one shall attain peace.
Upatiṣya said:

"The Leader has taught how the progression of the world possesses causes consisting of karma and afflictions, and he has likewise taught the cause for the cessation of that karma and those afflictions."
Having personally realized that supreme liberation in which the suffering inevitably bound to birth, old age, and decay does not abide, that bull among speakers proclaims it himself.

(Dutt 6) Then, right there, Kolita the wanderer attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena—an eye that is free from dust, free from stain, and free from secondary defilements—and he realized the fruit of stream-entry. He spoke thus:
"This is the crossing over the flood, the practice of reality; it is peaceful, a swift boat."

This supreme knowledge, which pacifies the three sufferings and leads to the further shore of saṃsāra, indeed destroys the aggregates and the afflictions and subdues Māra. This is true thorough understanding;
this is liberation, which washes away enmity and strife and dries up the ocean of suffering.
Kolita said, "Where does that Blessed One, the Buddha, dwell at present? Upatiṣya replied,

"I have heard, venerable sir, that the Blessed One is dwelling right here in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakanivāpa, together with the community of monks and the community of bodhisattvas."
Having heard this, he approached and sat down to one side.
"We two shall receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
Kolita said, "So be it, venerable sir; let there be the going-forth for both of us together with our retinues."

The two wandering mendicants, Upatiṣya and Kolita, together with their retinue of followers, approached the place where the Blessed One was. At that very instant, moment, and second, Māra the Evil One heard that in the regions of Aṅga and Magadha, the two noble men Upatiṣya and Kolita, who were endowed with renowned fame and glory, along with their retinues, desired to go forth into homelessness under the teaching of the ascetic Gautama.
[To seize them]. Having heard this, he thought:
"If these two become disciples of the ascetic Gautama, they will render my realm of Māra empty."
"Through conversation, I shall cause these two virtuous men to abandon their renunciation.
Then the evil one thought, "I shall approach them after assuming another disguise."
Then, at that very moment, Māra the Evil One quickly vanished from his own abode and approached those two noble men by way of the venerable Aśvajit’s appearance and attire;
having approached, he said this:
"All of this that was spoken by me is indeed false, being merely a semblance of reason and a cause."
It was only to ascertain the movement of your own minds that I spoke all this;
indeed, it is entirely useless, for there is no further cause here, nor how could there be the attainment or fruit of such auspicious action by this Kṛṣṇa?
"Quickly indulge excessively in the qualities of sensual pleasure; you two should find delight in play.
There is no death, nor birth, nor is there for you any world of suffering or old age.
There is no fruit of merit or demerit produced by action; in this matter, there is no cause or efficacy to ritual acts."
The son of the Śākyas speaks here for the sake of gain; do not proceed out of faith.
Then this thought occurred to Upatiṣya and Kolita:
"Surely it is Māra, the Evil One, who has approached us for the purpose of cutting short our going-forth.
Then Upatiṣya, turning his face away, summoned his own assembly and spoke thus.
Listen, O young men! Remember the defects of saṃsāra:
the world is oppressed by old age and surrounded by death.
In order to abandon both of these, you should properly take up the life of renunciation.
Then Kolita said to Māra:
"I have known that supreme one among the virtuous, the possessor of wisdom, whose Dharma brings an end to the three types of suffering."
There is no one at all who could ever divert us from this resolve;
with steadfast minds, we are always intent on the utterance of words for the sake of quenching craving.
Do not, like a lion in form, lead our minds astray with the words of a jackal.
And those deities who had seen the truths, remaining in the sky, gave their approval to those two noble men:
"Excellent, excellent, noble men! This path is renowned throughout all the world, namely, the going forth into homelessness;
this path is the pacification of all suffering."
"This path is the entry into the domain of all Tathāgatas; it has been praised by all the Blessed Buddhas. This path is lauded.
Then Māra, the Evil One, distressed, dejected, and full of remorse, vanished right there.

Then Upatiṣya and Kolita, the two wandering mendicants, looking at their own assembly, spoke these words: "O young men, you should know that we have set out for the homeless life, directed toward the Tathāgata, in order to reach the further shore of the ocean of old age and death."
"But whoever among you does not wish to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, let him turn back right here.
Then all those five hundred young brahmins said:
"Whatever we know, all of that is through the power of you two."
"Surely you two have gone forth into the religious life in a noble place! For whose sake you two have gone forth, for that same purpose shall we also go forth.
Then the wandering mendicants Upatiṣya and Kolita, with a retinue of five hundred, went forth into the religious life under the Blessed One.

Knowing that they had set out, Māra the Evil One manifested a great abyss outside the great city of Rājagṛha, extending for hundreds of yojanas below, so that the two might not be able to approach the presence of the ascetic Gautama.

But the Blessed One again manifested such a supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that those two wandering mendicants, Upatiṣya and Kolita, did not see that great abyss as they traveled along the straight path.

Again, Māra the Evil One manifested a mountain before the two of them—hard, solid, and impenetrable—and hollowed out a space a thousand *yojanas* in height; he also manifested a thousand lions that were fierce, wicked, and terrifying.
Yet, through the majesty and spiritual power of the Blessed One, those two noble beings did not see a single lion.
And they did not hear the lion’s roar;
rather, they proceeded by a straight path toward where the Blessed One was.
And the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Behold, monks, these two virtuous men, leaders of a group and surrounded by a retinue.
We behold them.
“We do, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “These two noble persons, together with their retinues, have been granted permission; they shall go forth in my presence.”
"Having gone forth, one of them shall become the foremost among all my disciples endowed with wisdom, and the second shall be the foremost among those possessing supernormal powers.
Then, at that time, a certain monk spoke these verses:
"These two wise men, who were prophesied by the Benefactor, the Supreme among Men, shall attend upon him."
Endowed with miraculous powers and confident in their wisdom, these two approach here out of reverence.
Then that monk, rising from his seat, together with many monks and many householders and renunciants, went out to meet those two good men and attended upon them.
Then those two good men approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, stood before the Blessed One, and said this to him:
"May we both receive from the Blessed One the going forth and full ordination into the state of a monk;
may we practice the holy life under the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What are your names, noble sons?
Upatiṣya replied,
"I am the son of the brahmin Tiṣya."
"My mother's name was Śārikā;
from her I was born,
and for that reason my name was made Śāriputra."
"I was previously granted permission by my parents for the sake of going forth.
Kolita said,
"My father's name is Kolita."
"My mother's name was Mudgalā;
therefore, the common name Maudgalyāyana was given to me. Some people know me as Kolita."
"Is there anyone named Maudgalyāyana?
"I was previously permitted by my parents to go forth.
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with their retinues, practice the holy life in my presence. This itself was their going forth and full ordination.
And not long after they had gone forth, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were together with their retinues.
Then Māra, the Evil One, assuming the form of Maheśvara, stood before the Blessed One and spoke thus:
"Those who are skilled in the practice of the meaning of the treatises and have reached the further shore of the sciences—all of them bow at my feet; I am their leader."
"O Gautama, come quickly for refuge to me, together with your circle of disciples, so that you may attain the desired nirvāṇa; I shall explain the clear path to you."
The Blessed One said:
"Your path carries this world toward miserable rebirths and leads it into the ocean of suffering;
my path, however, dries up the ocean of suffering for this world of moving and unmoving beings."
Why do you prattle on further with such bold and noisy insolence, you who have the voice of a wicked jackal?
You are utterly shattered; you are no longer able to perform the work of Māra against me here.

(Dutt 12) Then Māra, the Evil One, vanished from his form as Maheśvara and, standing once more before the Blessed One in the guise of Brahmā, spoke thus: "That which you have accomplished through your wisdom— the pacification of the sprouts of existence born of karma and afflictions— "
Since you, O Sage, endure such sufferings here once again solely for the sake of sentient beings,
there is no person anywhere in this world, O Lord, who is a more worthy recipient than yourself;
why then do you, free from all illness, not enter nirvana quickly, for that time has indeed come?
The Blessed One said:
"I behold beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who stand ready to be disciplined; out of compassion, they are to be fully liberated by me."
"The world has fallen into mediocre, superior, and inferior states, with liberation as its ultimate goal;
therefore, I shall lead it to nirvāṇa. Why then, O evil-minded one, do you invite me with deceit?"

Then again, Māra the Evil One, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, vanished from that spot and went to his own abode. Having entered a chamber of sorrow, he sat down. At that very moment, all the beings dwelling in the realm of Māra asked one another, "What is the cause for which our Great King has entered the chamber of sorrow and sat down, yet no one knows?"
Then five hundred daughters of Māra, taking up flower garlands and ointments that were most pleasing, and having adorned themselves with garments and ornaments that were most charming,

stood before the evil Māra playing divine musical instruments that produced supreme joy and delight; they danced, sang, and played with most charming voices, accompanied by a great divine orchestra of fivefold instruments suited for amorous play.
And that Māra, the Evil One, raising his arms, began to cry out, "Make no noise! Make no noise!
Though addressed in this way, they continued to sing and beat their musical instruments.

And Māra, the Evil One, once again raised both his arms and began to cry out, doing so up to seven times. The apsarases stood before Māra, the Evil One, engaged in amorous play; likewise raising both their arms, they cried out, "Make no sound! Make no sound!"
When they had been addressed in this way, those apsarases stood silent.
Then, the apsaras named Vidyudvalgusvarā, having bowed with palms joined toward Māra the Evil One, spoke thus:
"O Lord, what sign of your passing away have you seen here today? Or has the world today become as if engulfed by fire?"
Is there some enemy here whose strength exceeds yours? Or why do you not rejoice, but instead take refuge in grief?
Māra said:
"I have a powerful enemy who has subdued his mind; on this earth, there is a son of the Śākyas, well-trained in illusions."
If there were no one possessing the marks of greatness, then this realm of desire of mine would be rendered empty.
That apsaras said:
"O Lord, who here today is capable, through the power of means, strength, heroism, and prowess, of bringing about the ultimate destruction of that [ocean]?
Who, endowed with might and power, could exhaust the ocean of craving, which has the long shores of the triple world as its bonds?"
Māra said:
"His bow is held fast with the noose of generosity, vows, intention, compassion, and resolve; his bowstring is grasped by the supreme weapons of emptiness and signlessness."
He is the teacher who instructs on the complete cessation of existence, and he is favorable toward the tranquility of the path leading out from cyclic existence.
In empty villages and cities, in the depths of forests, and even in mountain caves, there are his disciples;
their minds are intent on meditation, they dwell in solitude, and they are constantly and properly engaged in the destruction of the afflictions.
Supported by their supernatural powers, strengths, and compassion, both Upatiṣya and Kaulita have been disciplined by the Sage;
having been well-trained in the Dharma through all the methods of the three worlds, they will indeed empty my realm of desire.

Then, having heard the praise of the Blessed One’s virtues from the presence of Māra, the Evil One, all those five hundred daughters of Māra attained the bodhisattva samādhi named *sarvākāravigatavidyun*.

Thereupon, those five hundred daughters of Māra cast divine musical instruments and divine flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and decorations toward where the Blessed One was, into the presence of the Blessed One.
And by the power of the Blessed One, those divine flowers, those divine musical instruments, and all those ornaments rained down upon the Bamboo Grove;
and those daughters of Māra themselves, along with their retinues, beheld them.
Upon seeing it, they themselves were filled with serene faith, wondering how such a rain of flowers had fallen in the Bamboo Grove. Then those monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, surely this kind of great, wonderful, and marvelous rain—never seen or heard before—has fallen because of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana together with their retinues?"
“Blessed One, what is the cause here? What is the condition?
The Blessed One said:

“This is not the power of these two sons of good family. Rather, O Evil One, five hundred female attendants from that abode of Māra have released this rain of great flowers, up to a rain of ornaments, right here.”
For the sake of my act of worship,
may these [beings] be long favorable to me;
they shall receive from me the prophecy regarding their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then those five hundred māra-maidens themselves heard the utterance of the Blessed One’s voice.
Having conceived faith toward the Blessed One, through that joy of faith they attained the samādhi called "Non-forgetfulness of the Thought of Awakening" (bodhicittāsaṃpramoṣa).
Then those māra-maidens, right there in the Veṇuvana grove, draped their robes over one shoulder and placed their right knees upon the ground.
Placing their joined palms upon the earth and gazing toward the direction in which the Blessed One was dwelling, they spoke thus:
"O sole eye of the world, you who have beheld the entire world as one whose eyes are failing, seeing it as a river of craving that must be dried up completely."
You are the savior of this world, including its humans and gods; O Sage, how may we ourselves quickly become Buddhas here?

O Blessed One, honored by men and gods, speaker of the ultimate truth: having cast off this loathsome female state entirely, may we, through your supernatural power, swiftly attain the supreme destination and, having gone there, hear the words of the Lord of Sages. Thus [may it be].
O Blessed One, proponent of selflessness, seer of the ultimate truth, whose lamp of speech is stainless and adorned with the jewels of the factors of enlightenment;
O peerless one, having drawn back the forces of Māra, now quickly grant me a prophecy for the sake of my awakening.
Then the daughters of Māra rose from their seats and, with one voice, spoke this verse to Māra the Evil One:
"You are indeed of wicked intent; having acted maliciously toward the Blessed One, how is it that you have obtained this fortune which is both unstable and insubstantial?
O you who are arrogant with pride, you have fallen into a terrible state, your entire form afflicted by the sufferings of birth and the rest."

Place your faith in the Victor, having thus cast away your anger; with your self extracted from the mire of pride and the defects of saṃsāra, may he—whose nature is known to the entire world—be yours. Come, let us proceed quickly to the Compassionate One.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One, whose mind was exceedingly wicked:
"What if I were to summon such a forceful surge of my own power as Māra that these five hundred female attendants would perceive themselves bound by the fetters of the five snares right here?"
Having returned to the forest, they would not be able to go back again;
[and Māra would not be able to bind them].
Why is that?
For those five hundred female attendants were sustained by the Tathāgata’s empowerment. Then, indeed, those five hundred female attendants departed from the presence of Māra, the Evil One.
Thereupon, this thought occurred to the wicked Māra, the Evil One:
Furthermore, I shall again call to mind such a surge of Māra’s power and domain, so that all this world will be enveloped by masses of Vairambha winds, great black clouds, and great black winds,
such that those very female attendants, bewildered in all directions and intermediate points, will not see the ascetic Gautama and will return once more to my abode.
Nevertheless, by the power of the Buddha’s empowerment, he was unable to produce even a slight breeze—such that it might at least cause the tip of a hair to quiver, let alone anything more extensive.
Then Māra the Evil One, becoming even more wicked, distressed, dejected, and full of remorse, cried out in a loud voice to his sons, hosts, and assembly;
he filled the entire realm of Māra with his sound.
"Come, dear sons, members of the assembly! We have fallen from our own domain and from our own power of supernatural success (*ṛddhi*).
This son of the Śākyas has arisen here within us like a poisonous tree; he is deceitful through his magic, though he speaks sweetly. (Rkp 1.29)

Then, at that sound, all those daughters of Māra, the daughters of Māra, and all the sons of Māra with their retinues and assemblies, appearing distressed and humbled, quickly approached from afar and stood before the Evil One.
And in that assembly, a son of Māra named Jayamati, having joined his palms in reverence, spoke thus:
"Why are you dejected, your mind so corrupted by supreme anger? Is there not for you the conflagration at the end of the aeon here, nor any falling away from this state?"
There is no enemy here who has grown so strong against you; why have you fallen into delusion, having suddenly lost your right mind?
Māra said:
"O son of the Śākyas, you do not see that low-born man seated beneath the tree; yet here before you, you speak these words: 'There is no powerful enemy for you.'"
All of us, along with our sons and retinues, have been bewildered many times by that deceitful one who possesses singular strength... // Rkp_1.31 //
Even those preeminent men in this world, whose fame and glory are renowned,
who are learned and entirely devoted to the composition of many treatises and poems— when they quickly went for refuge to that Son of the Śākyas, they were struck by the goads of the Dharma.
Yet this enemy of mine, who possesses a pleasing form but a deceitful mind, is being fought by me.
"Having abandoned these most beloved attendants, those pitiless ones have today gone for refuge to that ascetic, leaving behind my kingdom.
For this reason, this entire triple world has been made empty by that rogue through his deceit."
"Today, we shall reduce him to ashes here, swiftly and with great effort by our superior strength."
Then all those sons of Māra, together with their retinues, [with palms joined, said this]:
"So be it! We shall display all our supernatural power, strength, majesty, and miraculous transformations.
If we are able to reduce this son of the Śākyas to ashes, that would be well."
"If we are unable [to prevail], we shall go for refuge to him.
O Father, you yourself are our witness:

since we, surrounded by a great army, were previously defeated by this son of the Śākyas alone and without a second—despite his superior strength—how much more so now, when we are accompanied by many attendants and our vision is distracted?"
Māra the Evil One spoke thus:
"Go for now, gentle sirs;
if you are able to kill this ascetic Gautama, then return."
"Even if you are not capable, nevertheless come;
we shall protect our own abode.

Then, twelve *bimba* assemblies of Māra's retinue, having passed beyond that point and pervaded upwards for eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, displayed such a supernatural speed of power (*ṛddhi-vega*) as that of the Māra-force.
They displayed these things:
they filled all the sky over the four continents with great black clouds;
and with great black winds and falling meteors, they struck Sumeru, the king of mountains, with their hands.
They caused the entire world of four continents to tremble and uttered sounds of supreme terror,
such that the nāgas and great nāgas, the yakṣas and great yakṣas [were shaken], along with the whole great earth with its hills, crags, and mountains.

And Sumeru, the king of mountains, having perceived the trembling and knowing the agitation of the lakes, great lakes, rivers, streams, great rivers, and the great oceans, stood in the expanse of the sky. And that assembly of Māra, standing upon Mount Sumeru and the earth, conjured up a rain of the measure of a *yojana* and released it over Aṅga and Magadha.

And having conjured a great rain of clubs, nooses, javelins, *bhiṇḍipālas*, iron arrows, crescent-headed arrows, razor-faced arrows, razors, razor-edged arrows, razor-faced razors, razor-edged razors, razor-toothed razors, razor-toothed weapons, formidable vajra-razors, razor-toothed razors, razor-toothed weapons, razor-toothed faces, distorted faces, and a rain that was firm, harsh, rough, and coarse, they released it. Then, at that time, the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called "The Destruction of Māra’s Realm."

By means of which he transformed the entire rain of stone weapons into a rain of divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, *māndārava*, and great *māndārava* flowers—
and he transformed those sounds of various musical instruments into the sound of the Dharma,

the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Saṅgha, the sound of the perfections (*pāramitā*), the sound of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the sound of approaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and so on, up to the sounds of both with-grasping (*sopādāna*) and without-grasping (*nirupādāna*).
All the winds of dust and darkness were stilled.
Whatever grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, forest trees, earth, stones, and mountains existed here in this four-continent world-system, he presided over them all as the seven great jewels.
By his mere look, the Blessed One brought everything up to the Brahma-world under his control with his body, even unto its summit.
And from each individual mark of the Blessed One, such a radiance issued forth that by this radiance the entire great trichiliocosm was suffused with a vast light.

And all those in this great trichiliocosm—whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, or non-humans; whether belonging to the hells, to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama—all of them beheld the Blessed One.
And many hundreds of thousands of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans, stationed in the sky, scattered flowers, circumambulated him to the right, offered praise, and paid homage.
Many hundreds of thousands of millions of beings from the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama regained their mindfulness.

Recalling the roots of merit planted in the past and exclaiming "Homage to the Buddha," they passed away from those states of woe and were reborn among the gods. Then, having witnessed such a miraculous display by the Blessed One, the twenty-two hundred thousand sons of Māra together with their retinues conceived an exceeding faith in the presence of the Blessed One and approached where the Blessed One was.

Having approached together with those five hundred daughters of Māra, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and, joining their palms in reverence, addressed him with these verses: "O you of pure form, ocean of supreme and most beautiful wisdom, equal to Mount Meru of gold!"
Having spread throughout the world with your glory, you shine; we go for refuge to you alone as our protector.
For those whose path is lost and whose eyes are closed, you act like a torch, as the sun does for the world;
O Invincible One, we go for refuge to you, the caravan leader and sole kinsman of living beings.
O you whose treasury is enriched with unaccumulated wisdom, whose mind is liberated like the nature of space,
whose speech is pleasing due to a heart moistened by compassion— we go for refuge to you, Sarvārthasiddha.
You are the liberator from the wilderness of saṃsāra, the one who demonstrates cause and effect through their complete assembly;
abiding in loving-kindness, knowing the supreme method, and abiding in compassion—we go to you for refuge.
Attached to existence— which resembles an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water— through reliance on sense objects,
we go for refuge to that King of Physicians, the Lord of the World, who destroys the disease of ignorance.

You are the bridge that delivers one from the midst of the four floods; through the seven treasures, the goals, and the modes of conduct, you reveal the true path, O Kinsman of the World. We worship you here, who are endowed with compassion.
"Forgive us, O you of perfect wisdom, for the malice we harbored toward you. Accept this transgression, O Hero, O Lord; you are the sole kinsman in the world, the most preeminent."
Having indeed cast off the faction of Māra, we shall generate here the supreme mind of awakening;
we invite all sentient beings, so that we may attain unsurpassed awakening.
Show us your noble conduct so that we may practice the perfections;
by how many qualities, free from false speech, are beings endowed with them that they attain awakening?
May the flowers that we scatter before you become parasols in all directions;
may they rest upon the heads of the supreme among bipeds in those realms which are sources of happiness in every season.
Then indeed, the sons of Māra and the daughters of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, scattered loose flowers over the Blessed One.

Through the supernatural power of the Blessed One, those scattered flowers were transformed into many thousands of millions of billions of flower-parasols, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā.

Those various flower-parasols remained in the sky above the crown-joints of all the Buddhas dwelling and maintaining themselves in the ten directions; and those daughters of Māra themselves, along with their hosts and retinues, [remained there].
They saw,

in all the countless and immeasurable Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— staying, maintaining themselves, teaching the Dharma, surrounded by assemblies, speaking, blazing, and shining resplendent as they sat.
Those flower-parasols remained suspended in the sky above, at the level of their heads.
And those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were identical in color, identical in marks, identical in form, and identical in appearance;
they perceived only differences among those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their lion-thrones, in their assemblies, and in the magnificent arrays of qualities of their Buddha-fields.
And they did not hear the vocal range of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

And that assembly of Māra, having seen such a miracle through the very power of the Blessed One, was filled with supreme joy and faith; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.
Then, those ten groups of Māra’s sons, together with their hosts and retinues, returned to the abode of Māra and reported this account to the wicked Māra.
They reported in detail:
"Not even a single pore of that ascetic Gautama could be destroyed by him.
Furthermore, twenty thousand more went for refuge to him alone and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, becoming even more fierce, distressed, and dejected, and feeling regret, spoke thus:
"My fortune has departed and will not return to me so long as there is no destruction of the Śākya son's sovereignty.
Remaining silent, with our minds focused on no other thought, how shall we slay this son of the Śākyas today?"
Then Māra, the Evil One, being dejected, entered the chamber of sorrow.
This concludes the first chapter, titled "The Humiliation of Māra," from the *Ratnaketu* Mahāyāna Sūtra.

Then those daughters of Māra and the sons of Māra, together with their retinues and assemblies, implored the Blessed One at that moment:
"O Blessed One, we are seekers of such a vehicle as this, and of such wisdom, supernatural power, compassion, skillful means, and eloquence.
It is marvelous, O Blessed One, how the Tathāgata is endowed with such skillful means and wisdom!"
“Blessed One, endowed with what qualities does a person not fall into the hands of evil friends and swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
“Son of good family, a certain person here who is endowed with four qualities does not fall into the hands of evil friends and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
By which four?
Here, noble sirs, a son of good family does not grasp at any phenomena, nor does he take up any phenomenon anywhere;
he does not approach it, does not appropriate it, does not abide in it, and he neither conceptualizes nor discriminates—namely, with respect to the perfection of generosity.
While practicing, he does not attend to the fruit of giving; he does not grasp it, does not take it up, does not dwell upon it, and does not conceptualize or discriminate it.
This continues even as he practices in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), until he neither conceptualizes nor discriminates.

Furthermore, O gentle sirs, that son of good family does not become a proponent of a "sentient being" (*sattva*), nor a proponent of a "living soul" (*jīva*), nor a proponent of a "nourisher" (*poṣa*).

He is not a proponent of a person (*puruṣa*), nor a proponent of a self (*pudgala*); he does not mentally grasp the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), nor does he conceptualize it or discriminate it.
Furthermore, O gentle sirs, that son of good family does not grasp forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, nor does he conceptualize them or discriminate them.

Furthermore, noble sirs, that son of good family does not grasp at, nor even conceptualize or discriminate, the arising, the basis, the production, the ripening of the fruit, the conditions, the objects, the causes, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields of all the three times and the triple world.

Why is this? Because it must be accomplished through the empowerment of the practice of the knowledge of omniscience, by means of a yoga-practice without an object, which is free from all conceptualization and discrimination regarding objective domains.

O noble ones, all dharmas and omniscience are non-existent; they are soundless, signless, letterless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, characterless, unattached, objectless, invisible, secluded, selfless, indefinable, tranquilized in every moment, without darkness or light, without location, without domain, independent, without side or counter-side, inconceivable, beyond what is to be abandoned, free from stinginess, without proliferation, stainless, partless, nothingness, without an agent or an experiencer, without support, ungraspable, without representation, non-manifesting, and momentary.

"O noble ones, omniscience is equal to space; it must be practiced through the yoga of emptiness and non-apprehension, through the yoga of non-abiding, through the yoga of non-clinging, and through the yoga of being free from conceptualization and discursive thought.
O noble ones, a person endowed with these four qualities does not fall into the hands of evil friends and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"O noble ones, whoever seeks omniscience through the practice of the basis characterized by the total uprooting of attachment to all sense objects becomes attached to duality.
One whose mental resolve is attached to duality deceives omniscience.
In this regard, what is duality?"
That which presides over or grasps the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields through the investigation of their characteristics—
this duality contradicts omniscience.
The conceptualization of practice, its basis, and its fruit— this is duality.
The conceptualization of birth, existence, grasping, and sentient beings as a basis is duality.
The conceptualization of teaching, revealing, establishing, the path of speech, sounds, and verbal expression as a basis is duality.
The conceptualization of the observation of annihilation and permanence, and knowledge and the object of knowledge as a basis is duality.
The conceptualization based on the designations of "being," "life-force," "nourisher," "person," "individual," "agent," and "instigator" constitutes this duality.
That which adheres to and conceptualizes "the further shore" and "the near shore," as well as "appropriation" and "rejection," constitutes this duality.

O gentle sirs, any person or individual who seeks the knowledge of the Omniscient One adheres to the investigation into the arising and cessation of the notions of "I" and "mine" throughout the three times.
He forms a conceptualization and grasps; these two are obstacles to the knowledge of the Omniscient One.

It is, for example, as if a man seeking fire were to touch the ground, one seeking drink were to grasp fire, one seeking food were to grasp a stone, one seeking flowers were to grasp a robe, one seeking fragrance were to grasp a human corpse, or one seeking a robe were to grasp a cemetery. Likewise, one seeking clothing were to grasp... [the same applies].

"O gentle ones, one who desires plaster for a wall might as well grasp at the sky; even so, those who seek the knowledge of the Omniscient One by means of the dual basis of the practice of meditative absorption and the conceptual proliferation of attachment are in vain effort.
Now, at that very assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Dhāraṇamati who had gathered and was seated."
He extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and spoke thus:
"Blessed One, is it possible to fully awaken to a dharma that is ineffable?
The Blessed One replied:
This indeed is perfect awakening: that one knows what is ineffable.
Therefore, noble son, I shall speak to you;
if it is appropriate for you, explain it accordingly.
There exists a dual-characteristic entity which receives the name "omniscience.
He said:
"If I say that it exists, it will become eternal."
Now, if it were non-existent, I would say that there would be annihilation;
yet the Middle Way is perceived,
which is neither existent nor non-existent.
That knowledge which, regarding these [phenomena], is unattached, non-arising, inexhaustible, immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond darkness and light—this indeed is perfect awakening.
The bodhisattva Vidyunmati said:
"O Blessed One, that skill in entering into knowledge wherein there is neither coming nor going—this indeed is perfect awakening."

The Bodhisattva Vairocana said: "O Blessed One, where there is no characteristic of attainment, no clear realization, no direct realization, no tranquility, no pacification, no three times, no three vehicles, and no conceit regarding the propriety of vows— this alone is perfect awakening."

The bodhisattva Dhāraṇamati said: "O Blessed One, he who does not conceptualize or discriminate the triple world, nor the three fetters, nor the state of the three knowledges, nor the three vehicles, nor the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, nor [regards them as] decrease or increase, nor as conformity."
"This alone is perfect awakening.
The bodhisattva Vajramati said:

"That which is the dharma of ordinary persons, the dharma of those beyond training, the dharma of those in training, the dharma of śrāvakas, or the dharma of pratyekabuddhas—one does not conceptualize it, nor does one discriminate it."
"He performs the proper service; this indeed is perfect awakening.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
"He who investigates suchness by way of seclusion—this indeed is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"He who does not conceptualize the non-arising characteristic of all dharmas for the sake of attainment or for the sake of clear realization—this itself is perfect awakening.
The Bodhisattva Acintyamati said:
When one causes the very mind that investigates the three realms to enter into the mind itself, and does not perceive either of these two minds through investigation—this indeed is perfect awakening.
The Bodhisattva Arivijaya said:

"That which is not attached to any phenomena, is not drawn toward them, is not indifferent to them, does not resent them, does not crave them, is not deluded by them, does not grasp them, and is not released from them—this indeed is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha said:
"He who does not cling to merit or sin, and who does not conceptualize 'I' or 'mine' regarding the entry into the method of profound patience— this indeed is perfect awakening."
The youth Candraprabha said:
"O Blessed One, that which does not cognize all phenomena through tranquility, and does not perceive the intrinsic nature, accumulation, or increase of phenomena—this alone is perfect awakening.
The youth Khagamati said:
"That for which the arising and passing away of all darkness and light—the increase and decrease—do not occur within the mind and mental factors; this alone is perfect awakening.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"He who practices the perfections with triple purity through the yoga of non-apprehension, neither becoming attached nor becoming detached; this alone is perfect awakening."
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said:
"O Blessed One, he who is neither attached to nor detached from all phenomena understands the profound principle of the Dharma.
And he who understands does not accumulate, does not discard, does not draw in, does not draw out, and does not cause the diminution of any phenomenon whatsoever."

One does not, through conceptualization or discursive thought, produce or perceive ignorance or liberation, nor arising or passing away, nor decrease or increase, with respect to entities; this indeed is perfect awakening.
By this very method, there is perfect awakening to all things.
Then the Bodhisattva Kautūhalika said:
"Mañjuśrī, what is the purpose of the application of yoga?
For by this very entry into the suchness of the single principle, through the method of profound cultivation, there is the full comprehension of the knowledge of the omniscient one."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is being free from uneven views; it is right view without superimposition; it is honesty and straightforwardness without superimposition."
Being free from evil; being endowed with reverence for the guru;
being endowed with pleasant speech; being endowed with right livelihood; being endowed with freedom from all fetters; being endowed with compassion for all beings despite being reviled;

being endowed with the threefold restraint; being endowed with non-deceptive wholesome qualities; being endowed with non-quiescence [for the sake of others]; being endowed with the protection of the true Dharma; and being endowed with never abandoning any sentient being.

O son of good family, these twenty applications are for the sake of the knowledge of omniscience: the relinquishing of all things; the establishing of strength in weak beings; providing refuge and fearlessness to those who are terrified; enjoining those set out on wrong paths to the correct practice; patience and gentleness; the characteristic of being free from all grasping and attachment; the avoidance of the entire mass of passion and ignorance; and the non-superimposition regarding the avoidance of the ripening of the fruits of all dedications.
The application of the knowledge of omniscience occurs through entering the suchness of the distinctions among all syllables, sounds, noises, utterances, and speech;

it occurs through entering the suchness of the words of all Tathāgatas by means of entering the suchness of the words of other non-Buddhist teachers; it occurs through entering the suchness of the application of the perfection of wisdom endowed with all merit; and it occurs through entering the suchness of the arising and passing away of all grasping.

Or, by entering into the reality (*tathatā*) of all phenomena— characterized by the causes and conditions that serve as the basis for the three doors of liberation— one comes to understand the application of the knowledge of the All-Knowing One.
The Bodhisattva Kautūhalika said:

Mañjuśrī, to whatever extent one understands this profound method of the Dharma, at that time one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever—neither the phenomenon that would be taught, nor the one for whom it would be taught, nor the meanings, words, and syllables by which it would be taught or revealed. Furthermore, by means of the non-discursiveness of all phenomena being inexpressible, one enters into suchness; whether it be what is to be abandoned, what is to be cultivated, or what is to be fully understood, one awakens to the knowledge of the omniscient one.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This attainment of the knowledge of the omniscient one by you has been well-spoken through this single method."
Why is that? For all phenomena are indeed free from superimposition;

they have the limit of non-arising and non-destruction as their boundary, the limit of the non-arising of ignorance and nirvāṇa as their boundary, the limit of the non-arising of space and nirvāṇa as their boundary, and the limit of the ineffable as their boundary—all phenomena are thus.
All sentient beings are likewise.

All phenomena are proclaimed to be without a substantial limit (*dravyakoṭīka*), because their nature is entirely free from attachment. They are the limit of nothingness regarding the aggregates of all three times and the three realms; they are the limit of the emptiness of the three types of conditioned formations. The aggregates of phenomena, the aggregates of maturation, and so forth—the aggregates of diminution—are not substantial limits.
Endowed with all phenomena that are the limit of emptiness, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the ineffable meaning, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the knowledge of omniscience.

Furthermore, while this prophecy concerning the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience was being spoken, twenty thousand members of the retinue consisting of hosts of Māra’s daughters and Māra’s sons attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Abandoning their coarse bodies, they obtained mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
Furthermore, these twenty thousand attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
And ninety-two billion beings among gods and humans attained various and manifold bodhisattva patiences, meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and dhāraṇīs.
Then those twenty thousand bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who had attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, scattered and strewed divine flowers over the Blessed One.

Having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they spoke thus: "Behold, Blessed One, how through the power of association with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), all the roots of merit, skillful means, and mental orientations of sentient beings come to be."

The Blessed One said, "This should be seen as having karma as its condition. And for the sake of cutting through the doubts of those beings who had become curious, the Blessed One recounted this former account (*pūrvayoga*):
"Long ago, sons of good family, in the past, after immeasurable great eons (*mahākalpa*) had passed, in this very [world]..."

At that time, at that period, during the great eon called Dyutindharā, when the lifespan of beings was sixty-eight thousand years, there appeared in the world of four continents a Tathāgata named Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
while dwelling in this world afflicted by the five corruptions, was teaching the Dharma connected with the three vehicles to the fourfold assembly.
At that time, there was a king named Utpalavaktra, a universal monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents.
Then, at a later time, King Utpalavaktra, accompanied by his harem, his retinue, and his army,
approached the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One and scattered various flowers over the Blessed One.
Having performed worship with various perfumes and various incenses, and having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks, he praised him with these two verses:
"Exceedingly praised for your virtues by the *bhujaṅgas*, gods, and others; you who remove a multitude of faults."
And by what means does one who benefits the world with these seven riches become possessed of subtle intelligence? Please tell me.
O destroyer of the world’s darkness, maker of the lamp of tranquility, subduer of birth, old age, disease,
and the sorrow of existence— tell me, by what means does one who wards off the world from the path of ruin escape the path of Māra?
Then, indeed, O sons of Māra, that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī said this to King Utpalavaktra:
"A bodhisattva endowed with three qualities of a true person becomes one of subtle intelligence. Which three?"
With a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), he feels compassion for all sentient beings;
he exerts himself for the pacification of the suffering of all sentient beings like a mother.

He investigates all phenomena and so forth as being devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), devoid of a nourisher (*poṣa*), devoid of a person (*pudgala*), and as being equal in their lack of differentiation.

Endowed with these three qualities, a true person, a bodhisattva, becomes one of subtle intelligence. Furthermore, O Great King, endowed with another three qualities, a true person does not become entangled in the snares of Māra.
What are these three?

That is to say: he is free from anger toward all sentient beings; he does not look for an opportunity to find fault; he regards all sentient beings as worthy of offerings; he consists of an even perception.
He examines all phenomena through a single principle—that is, as equal to space, unconditioned, non-differentiated, unborn, unarisen, and unceasing.
By means of non-apprehension, he contemplates them all as being like space, devoid of substantial characteristics.
"Great King, a person endowed with these three qualities does not become entangled in the snares of Māra and is liberated from the path of Māra.
Then the chief queen of King Utpalavaktra, named Surasundarī, surrounded and escorted by eighty-four thousand women, approached the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.
Having approached, she scattered various flowers over that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī, and addressed him with these verses:
O bearer of incomparable qualities, dispeller of darkness, remover of rebirth, tell me how one becomes here a youth,
free from evil destinies, endowed with splendor, modest in mind, and swift in performing what is beneficial.

O Sugata who has reached the supreme goal, O Blessed One who brings about the delight of tranquility, how can a man here abandon that young woman? Tell me quickly, O well-disciplined one who acts for the benefit of others: pacify the extreme darkness from the sky of my vision.
O Śramaṇa, peerless in this world, supreme one whose multitude of virtues is renowned, upholder of mindfulness and discipline:
if I am indeed destined to become a man here, then quickly speak the nectar of the Sugata’s path, free from all darkness.

When this had been said, noble son, that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī spoke thus to his chief queen Surasundarī: "Sister, there is a method by which a woman quickly transforms her female state; her previously projected female state is swiftly and completely exhausted, and she no longer takes rebirth among women until her unsurpassed final nirvāṇa."
Except by means of one's own vow.
In this regard, sister, what is the method by which a woman quickly becomes a man and swiftly exhausts, without remainder, the female state previously projected?

Here, sister, is this dhāraṇī called Ratnaketu, which is of great purpose, great benefit, and great power; it brings about the end of all female states and [destroys] the corruption resulting from the ripening of suffering in body, speech, and mind.
It causes [the female state] to be eliminated without remainder. Furthermore,
by relying upon this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female nature of women passes away without remainder.
Having disappeared, the female faculty manifests as the male faculty.

Furthermore, that man becomes handsome, with all his limbs fully complete; he is upright and skilled in subtle knowledge. His actions of body, speech, and mind are well-performed, and he conducts himself with excellent conduct. He becomes a conqueror of all enemies.

Moreover, whatever ripening of the fruit of evil deeds of speech and mind there may be for him—whether experienced in this life or in future lives—that which results in the experience of suffering of body, speech, and mind comes to total exhaustion.

Excepting those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), those who reject the true Dharma, and those who slander the noble ones— for them, moreover, by that very state, their female nature is completely exhausted without remainder.

The maturation of the corruption of body, speech, and mind, which would otherwise result in a female existence as vast as Mount Sumeru in a future life— this karma-obstruction, this evil outflow, which is to be experienced as the ripening of suffering, is entirely exhausted and brought to an end.
Why is that?
Because this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī has been spoken by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas of the past;
it has been empowered, mutually rejoiced in, praised, extolled, and lauded for the sake of exhausting the karma of sentient beings that results in the ripening of suffering.
For the sake of increasing the roots of virtue,
there are certain Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside and maintain themselves in their respective Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
All those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, recite this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī and even praise it for the exhaustion of the karma of sentient beings and for the increase of their roots of virtue.

Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future in the ten directions, each in their respective worlds, they too shall speak this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī— indeed, they shall praise it— for the sake of exhausting the karma that results in the suffering of sentient beings and for the increase of their roots of merit.
I, too, shall now speak this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī.
And I shall praise and extol this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī as it is being spoken by the Tathāgatas currently residing in the ten directions.

Sister, if any consecrated Kṣatriya king who has attained power over his realm should write down this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī in a book and preserve it, for that Kṣatriya king there will be a sublime [splendor] in the ten directions.
His fame, renown, and verses of praise will arise;
he will fill the supreme realm of form with his noble reputation.
And many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas will follow behind that kṣatriya, remaining there for his protection and guardianship.
And in his realm, all the defects of strife, quarreling, famine, disease, foreign armies, adverse winds and rains, and extremes of cold and heat shall be pacified.
All malevolent yakṣas, rākṣasas, lions, buffaloes, elephants, and wolves shall become harmless.
And all defects that are poisonous, bitter, pungent, coarse, tasteless, harsh, and to be experienced as painful contact shall be pacified.
Furthermore, all his wealth, grain, medicinal herbs, trees, fruits, and flowers shall sprout, flourish, and become succulent and delicious.
If a consecrated Kṣatriya king, when a battle has arisen, should place this *Ratnaketu* dhāraṇī manuscript upon the tip of a banner, that consecrated Kṣatriya king will defeat the enemy host.

If two Kṣatriya kings, both consecrated and engaged in battle, should each have the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī manuscript fastened to the top of their banner, they will bring about mutual affection and harmony. Thus,
the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī possesses many such qualities wherever it may be— in a village or in a city.
In a village, or among humans, non-humans, or quadrupeds, should there be untimely death or affliction for those who are diseased,
this book of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī should be brought therein with great offerings and requisites.
Having brought it in, by one who is well-bathed, whose limbs are well-anointed, who is clothed in new robes, who observes celibacy, and who is strewn with various flowers—
Having ascended a lion throne that is perfumed with various fragrances and draped with various cloths, this manuscript of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī should be recited there.
All diseases and untimely deaths therein will be pacified;
and all fears, horripilation, and ill omens therein will vanish.
Whosoever among women should desire a son, she, having bathed and donned new robes, observing celibacy,

He shall obtain a son;
this will be his final existence as a woman, until his unsurpassed parinirvāṇa, except for the sake of ripening sentient beings through his own previous vow.

As soon as this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī was spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the great earth shook once again; and upon hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female characteristics of five hundred daughters of Māra disappeared and male characteristics appeared.

Upon hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female characteristics of immeasurable and incalculable thousands of goddesses, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas vanished, and male characteristics appeared;
and all of them developed a mind that never turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And all their karma conducive to obtaining future female rebirths was completely extinguished without remainder.
With palms joined, those women addressed the Tathāgata Śākyamuni with a loud voice, saying:
"Homage, homage to the Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the performer of wonders!"
"Speak with great compassion [in detail: how was our female state made to disappear and a male state, complete in all its aspects, produced]?

Through that wondrous miracle and its power of inspiration, may we generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. O Blessed One, speak this ancient account for the sake of surpassing the immeasurable and incalculable gods and humans."

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, spoke of a former connection: "O noble ones, at that time, in those days, Queen Surasundarī—the chief consort of King Utpalavaktra—along with eighty-four thousand women, heard this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī from the presence of the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī; by the mere hearing of it," [she attained this].
The female characteristics of that chief queen, the celestial beauty, and of those eighty-four thousand women vanished, and male characteristics appeared. Likewise,

for the innumerable and immeasurable daughters of the gods, and even for the daughters of humans and non-humans, upon merely hearing this *Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī*, their female organs disappeared and male organs appeared.
It appeared;

and for all those thousands of women, the karmic obstructions conducive to the future attainment of female form were entirely and completely suppressed. And when the chief queen of King Utpalavaktra, Surasundarī, together with her retinue, attained manhood—

Then King Utpalavaktra, the universal monarch and lord of the four continents, having consecrated his eldest son with the royal inauguration, went forth into homelessness together with his nine hundred and ninety-nine sons, including Surasundara; together with eighty-four thousand great men such as Surasundara,
and together with another ninety-two thousand followers, he departed into the presence of that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron-colored robes, he went forth from the home to the homeless life in perfect accordance with the Dharma.
Having gone forth, he became devoted to recitation and intent upon wise reflection (*yonisomanasikāra*).
Then, it occurred to many tens of millions of living beings there:
"Why has the Cakravartin king gone forth?
They said this to one another:
"This Tathāgata is engaged in the work of Māra; he is deceitful, a deceiver, and intent upon the work of Māra. (Dutt 45)
He teaches the Dharma;
for some he manifests the female form, and for others the male form.
For some he causes the hair and beard to be shorn;
for some he provides red robes, and for others, white ones;
for some he teaches the Dharma for the sake of rebirth as a deity.
He teaches the Dharma for some to be reborn as humans, for others to be reborn in the animal realm, and for others regarding death and rebirth;

he is devoted to the paths of Māra’s karma and possesses the illusion of assuming a female form. That ascetic Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī is a deceiver in the guise of an ascetic; let us therefore depart from here, lest we be captivated by his appearance and characteristics.
"May we see him, yet not hear even a single word from him.
Then, right there, a soldier named Kumārabhṛta spoke thus:
My wives, the women of the inner apartments, and my daughters—all of them had their female characteristics removed by this wretched śramaṇa Koṇḍañña and were transformed into male organs;
having shaved the heads of all of them, he provided them with red robes.
And I alone have become afflicted with grief.
"All of us together shall enter that rugged, vast, and dense mountain,
where we shall not even hear the sound of the voice of this crow-like ascetic, this deceptive ascetic who is ensnared by the snares of Māra, let alone see him."

They all, being satisfied, said, "So be it. Then Kumārabhṛta Bhaṭa, together with those many tens of millions of beings who had fallen into doubt, set out for a remote region, a rugged mountain wilderness, in the guise of a seer.
He practiced the conduct and taught the Dharma to those beings in this way:
"There is no liberation from cyclic existence; there is no ripening of the fruit of well-performed or ill-performed actions."
This ascetic is an advocate of annihilationism; he is engaged in the work of Māra and is a deceiver.
Those who approach him for a vision, those who pay him homage, and those who listen to his Dharma become distracted in mind;
moreover, he shaves their heads.
He banishes them from their homes,
gives them dyed robes,
and makes them practice the conduct of the charnel ground.
He establishes them in the practice of begging for alms;
he makes them eat but once a day;

their minds are free from uneven views, they are constantly vigilant, they delight in dwelling in seclusion, they are withdrawn into their dwellings, and they are devoid of sensual pleasure, dancing, singing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, finery, sexual intercourse, and the drinking of fermented or distilled liquors; they speak but little.

He acts in such a manner that, appearing in the guise of a śramaṇa, he has arisen as a proponent of annihilationism, intent upon the path of Māra, and become an enemy to sentient beings— such was the deed observed of this Śramaṇa Gautama, never before seen or heard.
By him, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings were made to adopt such an evil view.
Later, at another time, the great śramaṇa Utpalavaktra heard that in a certain mountain thicket, some...
Having heard that they themselves have set out upon a wrong path and are causing others to adopt this same perilous view, while spreading disrepute for the Three Jewels, it occurred to him:
"As long as I do not liberate beings from those evil states of view and establish them in right view, my life as a śramaṇa will be in vain."
"And how might I, in a future time when the world has become blind, realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
And how will I be able to liberate those beings who have fallen into calamity and are bound by the snares of the four Māras?
Then the great ascetic Utpalavaktra, possessed of immense and firm prowess and great compassion, [addressed] that Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī...

Having gazed upon the Tathāgata, surrounded and honored by hundreds of thousands of living beings, he wandered through various outlying villages, towns, cities, mountains, rugged terrains, and mountain hamlets, teaching the Dharma to those sentient beings here and there.
Having turned those beings away from evil views and established them in right view, he settled them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
some others he established in the aspiration for the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, some in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, and some in the [spiritual] fruits;
and some he caused to go forth into homelessness.
He established some in the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), some in the one-day fast (*upavāsa*), and some in the taking of the three refuges (*triśaraṇagamana*).
To the women, he taught this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī*,
and having caused them to turn away from their female state, he established them in manhood.

Furthermore, those who were not followers of the śramaṇa's path and had fallen into doubt regarding the Tathāgata— he led them all away from that evil state of wrong views, caused them to confess their transgressions, and established them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having brought him before that very Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī, he caused him to go forth into the religious life, setting aside the soldier Kumārabhṛta.
And by him, this vow was made:
"Just as this ascetic Utpalavaktra has led away and dispersed my assembly, so shall I also [attain] his unsurpassed..."
Having set out for perfect complete enlightenment, I would exercise the role of Māra in that Buddha-field; that is to say, from the time he is in the womb, I would harass him.

Thereafter, while he is a newborn infant, while he is engaged in childhood play, while he is occupied with the arts, crafts, and study, while he is in the midst of sensual pleasures and the inner apartments, and even until he is seated at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I would cause him terror.
"And may I create obstacles for him,
and once he has attained awakening, may I cause the destruction of his teaching.
Then that great ascetic, Utpalavaktra, [perceived] that the soldier Kumārabhṛta had thus reached a conclusion regarding his vow.
Then, having propitiated him through great hardship, effort, and valor, and having turned him back from that state of evil views,
he caused him to confess his transgression and inspired in him the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thereupon, the soldier Kumārabhṛta, his faith being subdued, made this aspiration:

“O Mahākāruṇika, when you have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then, having attained awakening, you should prophesy my own attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, O gentle-faced ones, you may perhaps have some doubt or uncertainty that at that time, on that occasion,
there was someone else named Utpalavaktra who [served] that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.”

Having performed manifold kinds of worship and service for him along with his retinue, he went forth into homelessness together with many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings; furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings were turned away from their states of evil views and established in the three vehicles.
An immeasurable number of beings have been established in the fruits [of the path],
and an incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions of women have attained manhood;
indeed, you should not view it in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the king named Utpalavaktra, a universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents. I formed this very reflection:

"O noble ones, whatever doubt or uncertainty you may have regarding that queen named Surasundarī who at that time and on that occasion obtained the state of a female ascetic (śrāmaṇya), it was I myself."
That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya was, at that time and on that occasion, he.

Now, friends, you might perhaps have some doubt or uncertainty that at that time and on that occasion there was another who was the soldier named Kumārabhṛta along with tens of millions of living beings;
however, you must certainly not view it in this way.
This Māra, the Evil One, was at that time and on that occasion a soldier named Kumārabhṛta. Because his attendant was ordained by me at that time, he conceived malice toward me and made this vow:
"When you have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then you shall prophesy my own attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Sons of good family, it was because you had conceived a lack of faith toward that very Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī,
and having spoken unrestrained words and embraced an evil view, that I myself liberated you from that evil view and ordained you.
Thereafter, in due succession,
you have attended upon many thousands of Buddhas and performed worship and service for them.
Having heard the Dharma from them, he made a vow and practiced the six perfections;
because of that, you previously experienced the sufferings of many eons in the three lower realms through the misdeeds of body, speech, and mind.
"By that very same karmic obstruction, they have now been reborn in the abode of Māra, the Evil One. Furthermore,
while this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-pūrvayoga* was being spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni,

the female state of those five hundred daughters of Māra vanished and they attained the male state, and they also acquired the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The minds of immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of beings, including gods and humans, were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
they became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Likewise, immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of beings became irreversible from the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The female state of countless and incalculable daughters of gods and humans was brought to an end, and they attained the basis of the male state.
This concludes the second chapter, titled "The Previous Life of Ratnaketu," from the Mahāyāna Sūtra. // 2 //
